claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure containing nanoscale precipitates embedded in a matrix.
Precipitate size distribution, volume fraction, and interfacial area density adequately represent the alloy's hierarchical microstructure.
A machine-learning model can combine experimental microstructural descriptors with outputs from a limited set of high-fidelity simulations.
The proposed model will predict Young's modulus under tensile testing.
The proposed model will predict yield strength under tensile testing.
The proposed model will predict fracture-related behavior, including crack initiation or propagation metrics.
The proposed model will be more accurate than conventional atomistic or continuum simulations.
The proposed model will have at least 20% lower computational cost than traditional simulation methods.
Machine learning can learn quantitative relationships between physics-related structural features and macroscopic mechanical properties.
Combining experimental microstructural data with simulation-derived outputs captures multiscale heterogeneity in HfNbTiVAl10.
Avoiding a full-scale simulation for every prediction reduces computational expense.
Heterogeneity effects are critical determinants of the alloy's mechanical behavior.
Conventional simulations are too computationally intensive or insufficiently accurate for hierarchical heterogeneity in HfNbTiVAl10.
The model may fail when hierarchical microstructural features evolve substantially under extreme testing conditions.
The model may fail when its experimental microstructural descriptors cannot be measured accurately.
The model may fail for alloy compositions, processing conditions, or testing conditions outside the training distribution.
Predictive gains depend on the quality and representativeness of the training data.
